# Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being {.unnumbered}

Imagine choosing between a secure job and a new venture. The job provides a reliable income; the venture offers independence while putting that income at risk. Even with a clear forecast of success, you must give up something you value. And the option that feels exciting today must eventually fit an ordinary working week. How should a choice account for both the future we imagine and the life we will actually live?

Part III connects uncertain outcomes to the lives in which they occur. It starts with the comparison of risky options and shows why a gain or loss depends partly on the point from which it is judged. It then examines what experience teaches us and leaves unseen, before turning to the mental accounts through which we organize gains, losses, and spending. From there, we ask why choices change as their rewards or costs move closer in time.

Plans also meet familiar routines. A student who intends to write may keep checking his phone, even when checking brings little enjoyment; the habit chapter examines why the response persists. The final chapter asks how choices contribute to daily experience, satisfaction, relationships, and meaning. Together, these chapters help us compare the future we imagine with the behavior and life a choice may actually produce.

[]{#fig-part-3-route}

## Questions to carry forward

- What consequences am I comparing, and from which reference point?
- What changes between making a plan and carrying it out?
- What aspect of life is this decision meant to improve?

Many of those consequences depend on other people. Part IV examines choices whose outcomes are shaped by what others believe, value, and do.
